Environment-free Synthetic Data Generation for API-Calling Agents

Seanie Lee    Sanjoy Chowdhury    Chao Jiang    Cheng-Yu Hsieh    Ting-Yao Hu    Alexander Toshev    Oncel Tuzel    Raviteja Vemulapalli Affiliation: Apple
August 24, 2026
Abstract

Training API-calling large language model (LLM) agents demands massive amounts of high-quality trajectories. However, collecting such data at scale typically requires fully implemented environments with executable APIs and realistic, pre-populated backend databases, creating a major bottleneck for scalability. To overcome this, we propose an environment-free synthetic data generation approach that leverages LLMs as on-the-fly digital world models. Given only API specifications, our method generates trajectories mimicking interactions between an agent and a stateful environment. Specifically, an LLM first generates diverse tasks solvable with the provided APIs. A teacher agent then iteratively solves each task while an LLM simulator generates coherent synthetic API responses conditioned on the task context and simulation history. Finally, an LLM judge filters the trajectories to ensure the quality of the resulting dataset. We evaluate our approach on the challenging AppWorld and OfficeBench benchmarks, which include both information-retrieval and state-changing tasks. Fine-tuning models on our synthetic data yields significant performance gains, demonstrating that effective supervision for API-calling agents can be generated without any executable environment. Our results establish LLM-based API simulation as a practical, scalable solution for training agents across diverse API ecosystems.

1 Introduction

The rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs) has driven a paradigm shift from passive text generators to active, API-calling agents (Schick et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2023). These agents fulfill complex user requests by executing API calls and reasoning over environmental feedback. However, training such agents requires vast amounts of high-quality trajectory data that capture the full multi-step interaction process, including user instructions, sequences of interleaved read and write API calls, execution results, and final responses. Compared to standard instruction-tuning data, these multi-step trajectories are substantially harder to collect at scale, yet they remain essential for teaching agents robust API usage, accurate state tracking, and effective error recovery.

Given the difficulty of manual collection, synthetic data generation has emerged as a natural solution, with recent works leveraging LLMs to produce agentic trajectories at scale (Qin et al., 2024; Zeng et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026). However, these works assume access to fully implemented environments with executable APIs and backend databases filled with realistic underlying states. This tight coupling between environment creation and data synthesis creates a major scalability bottleneck. To generate training data for a new set of APIs, one must first engineer the corresponding infrastructure and, more challengingly, source the diverse underlying state configurations required to populate the environment.

In this work, we ask a fundamental question: can we generate high-quality agentic trajectory data without building the underlying environments at all? Our key conjecture is that modern LLMs, having been pretrained on vast corpora of world knowledge, can function as dynamic digital world models. Given API specifications, input arguments, task instructions, and prior interaction history as context, an LLM can synthesize realistic execution results that mimic feedback from a live environment, accurately reflecting the underlying state changes. Driven by this insight, we introduce a highly scalable paradigm for agentic data generation. Instead of constructing real environments and executing actual APIs, we use LLMs to simulate all environmental feedback on-the-fly directly from API specifications.

To instantiate this paradigm, we propose ESAT, an Environment-Free Synthetic Agentic Trajectory generation pipeline that uses only API specifications as input. The pipeline operates in three stages, as illustrated in Figure 1. First, during the task synthesis stage, an LLM generates diverse, realistic tasks solvable by the target APIs, with an LLM-based critic filtering out invalid tasks. Second, the core trajectory synthesis stage pairs a teacher agent with our LLM-based API simulator. As the teacher iteratively issues API calls to solve the task, the simulator seamlessly generates coherent environmental feedback on-the-fly using the user task and prior simulation history as context. This interaction produces complete, multi-step agent trajectories entirely in simulation, without ever requiring an executable environment (see Appendix L for example trajectories). Finally, during trajectory filtering, an LLM judge evaluates the generated trajectories for correctness, completeness, and redundancy, discarding sub-optimal samples to ensure a high-fidelity training dataset.

ESAT offers two critical advantages. First, it turns agentic trajectory synthesis into a lightweight specification problem. By relying solely on API specifications rather than fully implemented environments or real-world deployed services, it allows data generation to scale seamlessly across diverse API ecosystems. Second, leveraging the long-context capabilities of modern LLMs, our simulator maintains state coherence across successive API calls, allowing for the generation of rich, multi-turn training trajectories that go far beyond isolated API-calling examples.

To validate ESAT, we conduct extensive experiments on AppWorld (Trivedi et al., 2024) and OfficeBench (Wang et al., 2024), two challenging multi-app benchmarks that evaluate agents on complex, multi-step information-retrieval and state-changing tasks. Our experiments across models ranging from 1.7B to 27B parameters demonstrate that supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on ESAT data leads to significant performance improvements with respect to the corresponding base models, yielding up to 50.5% on AppWorld and 60.5% on OfficeBench. Most notably, on AppWorld, which provides an official set of training tasks, models trained on ESAT data outperform the models trained on the training task trajectories collected from the real AppWorld environment.

Our contributions are summarized below:

  • •

    We introduce a context-aware, LLM-based API simulator that acts as a dynamic digital world model. By leveraging task context and interaction history, this simulator generates coherent environmental feedback, enabling the synthesis of complex, multi-step, API-calling trajectories without any real API execution.

  • •

    We propose ESAT, a novel, environment-free data synthesis pipeline that reduces agentic trajectory generation to a lightweight specification problem. By requiring only API specifications as input, ESAT eliminates the infrastructure and data bottlenecks associated with building and populating executable environments, enabling seamless scaling across diverse API ecosystems.

  • •

    We demonstrate that ESAT data is highly effective for supervised fine-tuning. Across models ranging from 1.7B to 27B parameters, our synthetic data drives substantial gains on AppWorld and OfficeBench datasets.

2 Related Work

Synthetic data with functional environments.

Because gathering human-annotated interaction data is notoriously resource-intensive, recent research trends have shifted toward LLM-driven generation. A variety of contemporary works now utilize LLMs to automatically synthesize agentic trajectories at scale (Qin et al., 2024; Zeng et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026). To ensure data fidelity, these approaches execute generated tool calls against live API endpoints or fully implemented sandboxes. While effective for generating grounded trajectories, these methods are fundamentally constrained by their dependence on functional environments. Adapting these pipelines to new APIs requires building bespoke backend infrastructures and painstakingly sourcing the diverse state data required to populate them. Consequently, this overhead severely limits the speed and breadth with which these methods can scale to new API domains.

LLM as an API simulator.

To bypass the bottleneck of executable backends, several existing works employ LLMs to simulate API responses. Early works such as ToolAlpaca (Tang et al., 2023) and ToolACE (Liu et al., 2025), and recent efforts like Nemotron (Chandiramani et al., 2026), synthesize multi-turn data by prompting LLMs to generate mock execution results. However, these methods rely on the LLM’s implicit conversational coherence, which leaves them vulnerable to state drift and hallucinated identifiers in long, complex trajectories. Other approaches tailor simulation to specific use cases: ToolEmu (Ruan et al., 2024) emulates outputs for safety evaluation, while StableToolBench (Guo et al., 2024) uses a GPT-4 simulator as a fallback for the offline evaluation of read APIs. The closest work to ours is Simia (Li et al., 2025), which utilizes simulated environments for agent training by augmenting seed trajectories for SFT and replacing real environments with simulated feedback during RL.

ESAT differs from prior simulation pipelines in four key ways. First, while most simulators focus on read APIs (Tang et al., 2023; Guo et al., 2024), ESAT supports state-changing write APIs, enabling interactions within dynamic, stateful environments. Second, unlike methods requiring pre-compiled API pools (Liu et al., 2025), existing benchmarks (Chandiramani et al., 2026), or seed trajectories (Li et al., 2025), ESAT generates both tasks and trajectories from scratch using only API specifications, making it seamlessly adaptable to new API domains. Third, instead of generating a full trajectory in a single LLM pass as in Li et al. (2025), ESAT uses explicit, step-by-step interactions between separate agent and simulator LLMs to generate multi-step trajectories. Fourth, to ensure state consistency across these long trajectories, the ESAT simulator validates each simulated response against the full interaction history, thereby acting as a persistent digital world model.

3 Method

In this section, we present ESAT, our environment-free pipeline that transforms API specifications into a dataset of multi-step, API-calling trajectories without relying on real API execution, backend infrastructure, or human-written tasks. As illustrated in Figure 1, the ESAT pipeline consists of three stages: (i) task synthesis from API specifications, (ii) trajectory synthesis using a teacher agent paired with an LLM-based API simulator, and (iii) trajectory filtering via an LLM judge.

3.1 Task Synthesis

This stage generates diverse user tasks solvable using the available APIs. The sole required input is a set of API specifications detailing each API’s name, purpose, and input/output schemas.

Bucketized generation.

To ensure broad and balanced coverage, task generation is organized into a combinatorial grid of configuration buckets. Each bucket is defined by a tuple of attributes, including difficulty level (e.g., easy, medium, hard), action type (e.g., read, write, mixed), task focus (e.g., constraint satisfaction, derivation), the number of apps (1, 2, or 3), and a range of APIs per app. These buckets are processed in a randomized sequence, and a task generator LLM is prompted multiple times to yield a desired number of tasks per bucket. During each invocation, we randomly sample apps matching the bucket’s required number and provide their full API specifications to the LLM, alongside the target difficulty, action type, task focus, and API count. The LLM then generates a task along with the list of APIs required to solve it. Detailed descriptions of the configuration attributes and their values are provided in Section G.1.

Inverse frequency-based sampling.

To ensure uniform coverage of apps and APIs, we employ an inverse frequency-based sampling strategy. We maintain running usage counts for every app and API across all generated tasks. When selecting apps for a generation step, we sample them with probabilities inversely proportional to their current counts, thereby prioritizing underrepresented apps. Furthermore, we rank all available APIs within the selected apps based on their counts, and explicitly instruct the task generator LLM to focus on the least-used APIs.

Task filtering.

Each generated task is evaluated by an LLM judge to ensure it is well-formed, solvable, and consistent with the corresponding bucket configuration.

Task rewriting.

Tasks generated directly from API specifications can sometimes suffer from procedural verbosity, outlining detailed instructions rather than natural goals. To address this, all tasks accepted by the judge are subsequently rewritten by an LLM to compress any procedural scaffolding into concise, intent-level requests that reflect actual user needs. These rewritten tasks are then verified by an LLM judge to ensure they remain valid. Section G.4 provides examples illustrating the impact of this rewriting process. If a rewritten task is rejected by the judge, the corresponding initial task is retained for trajectory synthesis.

3.2 Trajectory Synthesis

In this stage, a teacher LLM agent iteratively solves each task by issuing API calls, while an LLM-based API simulator dynamically generates synthetic responses. This yields complete, multi-step training trajectories that include the agent’s reasoning, API calls, and simulated environmental observations, all without executing any real APIs. Example trajectories are provided in Appendix L.

To ensure structural correctness and semantic coherence, the simulator LLM conditions its output on a rich input context, which includes: (1) the full API specification, (2) the API call arguments, (3) the task being solved, (4) the history of previous API calls in the trajectory and their simulated responses, (5) the name, email, and phone number of a virtual user, and (6) the current date and time. To prevent overly long input contexts and accelerate simulation, we restrict the simulation history to previous API calls from the same app.

Rules for the simulator.

The simulator LLM is guided by four core rules encoded in its system prompt: (1) Data consistency: it must preserve state across turns (e.g., a song assigned to a specific artist earlier must remain under that artist); (2) Data diversity: listed results should contain a mix of task-relevant and irrelevant items to mirror real-world noise; (3) Data realism: generated values must respect field constraints such as numeric ranges and unique identifiers; and (4) Schema compliance: responses must strictly conform to the schema provided in the API specification.

Simulation quality checks.

To ensure that the simulator produces accurate and realistic responses, we employ multiple stages of quality control. Before invoking the simulator LLM, the API call arguments are programmatically validated for missing parameters and type mismatches. If errors are detected, the simulator directly returns an appropriate error message without invoking the LLM. For valid API calls, the LLM-generated response undergoes multiple checks. First, it is programmatically verified against the expected output schema. In the event of a schema mismatch, the simulator LLM is re-prompted using the schema errors as feedback. Once the response passes the schema check, it is evaluated for semantic correctness and consistency with the simulation history using the same LLM as a judge. If the judge identifies any errors, the simulator LLM is prompted to refine its response using the judge’s output as feedback. Only responses that pass all checks are returned. We allow a fixed number of refinement steps; if the simulator fails to generate a valid response after exhausting all retries, we declare a simulation failure.

Trajectory termination.

Trajectory generation for a task concludes when the agent explicitly calls a special task completion API, exceeds a predefined limit on the number of execution steps, or invokes an API from an app that was not used to synthesize the corresponding task. The process also halts if the simulator fails.

3.3 Trajectory Filtering

Trajectories in which the agent finished the task by calling the task completion API are finally evaluated using a trajectory-level LLM judge, which decides whether the agent correctly solved the corresponding task. Each trajectory is judged multiple times, and we retain only those with a majority-positive verdict.

All the LLM prompts used for data synthesis are provided in Section H.7.

4 Experiments

Benchmarks.

We evaluated our approach on two challenging, multi-app benchmarks designed to test complex API interactions. AppWorld (Trivedi et al., 2024) provides a rigorous testbed of intricate tasks that require agents to coordinate numerous read and write API calls across multiple apps. The environment features 457 APIs distributed across nine everyday apps, with the average task necessitating 10 unique APIs and 45 total calls. AppWorld provides two test splits: Test-Normal (Test-N) with 168 tasks and Test-Challenge (Test-C) with 417 tasks. The latter introduces two held-out apps to evaluate generalization under increased difficulty. OfficeBench (Wang et al., 2024) focuses on office automation, featuring 20 APIs across eight apps. Tasks require agents to plan long-horizon workflows across apps, such as extracting spreadsheet data, scheduling calendar events, and dispatching emails. Following Li et al. (2025), we excluded OCR-dependent and unsolvable tasks, evaluating on 26 two-app and 46 three-app tasks.

Models.

We used GLM-4.7-FP8 (Zeng et al., 2025) for task synthesis, GLM-5.1-FP8 (Zeng et al., 2026) for trajectory synthesis (the teacher agent and API simulator), and Gemini-3.1-Pro (Google DeepMind, 2026) for trajectory filtering. The resulting synthetic data was used to fine-tune eight models: Qwen3 (1.7B, 4B, 8B, and 14B) (Yang et al., 2025) and Qwen3.5 (2B, 4B, 9B, and 27B) (Qwen Team, 2026).

Training.

Each training trajectory was formatted as a multi-turn conversation consisting of the task instruction, the agent’s reasoning and API calls, and the simulated API responses. We followed a standard SFT strategy, training the model to predict the agent’s output in each turn conditioned on the task instruction and all previous API calls and their responses. Detailed training hyperparameters are provided in Appendix D.

Evaluation.

All results reported in this section are averaged over eight inference runs, with standard deviations presented in Appendix F.

4.1 Results on AppWorld Benchmark

ESAT training data from AppWorld APIs.

We generated 9K trajectories using 340 APIs from AppWorld, restricting our selection to seven apps to strictly exclude the two held-out apps in the Test-C split. This dataset is denoted as ESAT-AW7. Further details regarding this dataset can be found in Appendix A.

ESAT training data from synthetic APIs.

To increase data diversity, we defined 52 novel synthetic apps with 1017 APIs independent of AppWorld, and used these APIs to generate 6K trajectories. These new apps were created by directly prompting Gemini to generate API specifications covering diverse domains such as e-commerce, productivity, travel, entertainment, and finance. We denote this synthetic app-based dataset as ESAT-S52. Further details regarding app synthesis and dataset statistics are provided in Appendix K and Appendix B.

AppWorld training data.

The AppWorld dataset provides a training set of 90 tasks. We generated eight trajectories for each task using the GLM-5.1-FP8 model as an agent in the real AppWorld environment, and used the task verifiers included in the dataset to filter for successful trajectories. The resulting 634 trajectories are referred to as the AWT dataset.

Metrics.

Following Trivedi et al. (2024), we report the task and scenario goal completion (TGC and SGC). Due to space constraints, we present the TGC results in this section and defer the SGC results to Appendix F.

4.1.1 Effectiveness of ESAT Data

Table 1 presents the performance improvements achieved by fine-tuning models of various sizes on different training datasets.

Strong generalization to new APIs.

Fine-tuning on the ESAT-S52 dataset, which was generated using 52 synthetic apps independent of AppWorld, results in substantial gains (8.4–47.0%) across all models. These results confirm that, when seeded with a diverse set of synthetic API specifications, the ESAT pipeline can generate effective training data that imparts robust API-calling skills capable of generalizing to unseen APIs. Notably, for almost all the models (except Qwen3-1.7B), the performance achieved with ESAT-S52 data surpasses that achieved using AWT data collected from the real AppWorld environment, despite ESAT-S52 being generated entirely from synthetic apps.

Large gains with minimal target information.

Fine-tuning on the combined ESAT-S52-AW7 dataset (which merges ESAT-S52 and ESAT-AW7) further improves performance in nearly all settings (up to 11.2%). The ESAT-AW7 subset provides additional synthetic trajectories generated using minimal target-domain information, relying solely on the API specifications from seven AppWorld apps.

For all models, fine-tuning on ESAT-S52-AW7 data leads to consistently better performance (0.7–15.3%) when compared to fine-tuning on AWT data. This demonstrates that highly effective, domain-specific supervision can be generated while entirely bypassing the need for the target environment during training.

Furthermore, fine-tuning on both ESAT-S52-AW7 and AWT data outperforms training solely on AWT data by significant margins (4.1–15.3%) for the Qwen3 models. For the Qwen3.5 models, augmenting the ESAT data with AWT data does not yield further performance gains. These results establish that the ESAT pipeline provides highly valuable supervision even when real-environment data is available.

Effective knowledge transfer.

When fine-tuned on the ESAT-S52-AW7 dataset, the Qwen3 (8B and 14B) and Qwen3.5 (4B, 9B, and 27B) models outperform the significantly larger GPT-4o (Hurst et al., 2024) and Nemotron-3-120B (Chandiramani et al., 2026) baselines, and the Qwen3.5-27B model achieves a performance that is comparable (< 3% difference) to the substantially larger GLM-5.1-FP8 teacher model. This demonstrates the efficacy of our approach for knowledge distillation, confirming that complex API-calling capabilities can be transferred to smaller models using purely synthetic, environment-free data.

Generalization to novel user data patterns.

During trajectory generation, our API simulator functions as a digital world model, dynamically simulating the underlying states of a virtual user for the specific task being solved. Consequently, the synthesized data patterns are entirely independent of those in the AppWorld environment. The large performance gains observed on the AppWorld test splits indicate that models trained on ESAT data successfully generalize to unseen user states and data distributions.

4.2 Results on OfficeBench Dataset

ESAT training data.

Since OfficeBench is an evaluation-only benchmark without a training set, we generated 1.7K trajectories using 20 APIs from OfficeBench, spanning eight apps. This dataset is denoted as ESAT-OB. Further details regarding this data are provided in Section C.1.

Metric.

Following Wang et al. (2024), we report the pass rate, defined as the percentage of tasks whose outputs satisfy the customized evaluation function (exact matching, fuzzy matching, or execution-based) associated with each task.

Effectiveness of ESAT data.

Table 2 presents the performance gains achieved by training on our environment-free synthetic data. The substantial gains (5.2–60.5%) once again confirm that highly effective supervision can be generated for API-calling agents while completely bypassing the need for a training environment. Notably, smaller models such as Qwen3-4B and Qwen3.5-4B are able to outperform the much larger Nemotron-3-120B and GPT-4o models. We also outperform Simia (Li et al., 2025), a recent work that focuses on synthetic API-calling data, by a significant margin (20% or more).

4.3 LLM Judge Quality

To understand the effect of the judge model used for trajectory filtering, we performed an ablation study comparing GLM-5.1-FP8 and Gemini-3.1-Pro. Table 3 shows the performance of the Qwen3-8B model trained on ESAT-S52-AW7 data filtered by each of these models. Compared to an unfiltered baseline, employing GLM for trajectory curation actually degrades the performance. In contrast, Gemini proves to be a highly effective filter. By aggressively discarding a larger proportion of low-quality trajectories, it ultimately yields superior downstream performance.

Correlation with real-environment correctness.

To quantify how well our LLM judge corresponds to true executable correctness, we conducted an empirical validation against the real AppWorld environment. We generated 720 trajectories (8 per task across the 90 AppWorld training tasks) using GLM-5.1-FP8 as the agent, and obtained ground-truth trajectory labels from AppWorld’s execution-based verifiers. We then re-evaluated these trajectories using our LLM judge, Gemini-3.1-Pro. The judge achieved a precision of 95.2%, confirming that when our pipeline flags a trajectory as correct, it is highly likely to be genuinely correct. This is the property that matters most for data curation, as it bounds the proportion of erroneous trajectories admitted into the training set.

Agreement with human annotators.

To further validate the trajectory filtering stage, we conducted a human evaluation of our LLM judge. We randomly sampled 200 trajectories (100 accepted and 100 rejected by the judge) and had human annotators assess them using the same grading criteria (see ). Annotators disagreed with the judge on only 8 accepted and 2 rejected trajectories, yielding a 95% overall agreement rate and a Cohen’s kappa of 0.90. This near-perfect agreement confirms the high fidelity of our filtering process and, by extension, of our curated ESAT training data.

4.4 API Simulator Quality Analysis

While the previous section establishes the effectiveness of our simulator-based ESAT pipeline in terms of downstream model performance, this section evaluates the quality of the simulator as a standalone component. To this end, we take 1K successful trajectories generated using AppWorld APIs, comprising approximately 27K simulated API calls. We evaluated the simulated responses of all these calls using GPT-5.1 (OpenAI, 2025) as a judge.11 1 To mitigate potential LLM-as-a-judge bias, we performed the same analysis using another frontier model and observed similar trends. Large-scale human evaluation of such data is prohibitively expensive and time-consuming. For each API call, the judge was provided with the history of simulated call responses (which was used as the simulator’s input context) and validated whether the current simulated response was consistent with the API specification, the call arguments, and the accumulated state from previous calls. According to GPT-5.1, our simulator produced valid responses for 93.7% of the calls, confirming the high quality of our ESAT training dataset.

Effect of response length.

Figure 2 shows how the simulation failure rate varies with the length of the simulated response. For short responses under 500 tokens, the failure rate remains low (2–3%), indicating that the simulator reliably produces well-formed responses when the required output is compact. The failure rate then rises steadily with length, reaching 8% in the 500–1K range, 18% for 1K–2K tokens, and 23% beyond 2K tokens. This trend could be due to the inherent limitations of the GLM-5.1-FP8 model used as the simulator in this work, and it could potentially be addressed by using more powerful frontier models that are better at maintaining consistency in long-form generation.

We also investigated the effect of input context length on failure rate and observed no significant correlation.

4.5 Comparison with Existing Synthetic API-calling Datasets

We compare the ESAT dataset against three existing synthetic API-calling datasets. The ToolAlpaca (Tang et al., 2023) and ToolACE (Liu et al., 2025) datasets target simple API-calling scenarios and do not model a stateful environment; specifically, their instances do not require coordinated read/write sequences over an evolving environment state. Nemotron (Chandiramani et al., 2026) is a recent work that scales synthetic API-calling data to 1.5M trajectories, but its API simulator generates each response at the turn level against a correctness rubric rather than a maintained state. Furthermore, its single-and multi-turn scenarios are not designed for the long-horizon, multi-app workflows present in AppWorld and OfficeBench. In contrast, ESAT’s simulator acts as a stateful digital world model that maintains a consistent virtual state across all API calls within a task.

Table 4 and Table 5 compare the effectiveness of these synthetic API-calling datasets in terms of downstream performance on the AppWorld and OfficeBench datasets, respectively. Finetuning models on the ToolAlpaca and ToolACE datasets yields performance that is similar to or worse than the corresponding zero-shot accuracy, while finetuning on the Nemotron dataset leads to only marginal performance gains in some cases. This clearly demonstrates that these simple tool-calling datasets do not equip agents with the skills needed to navigate complex, stateful environments. In contrast, training on the ESAT dataset leads to substantial performance gains on both benchmarks. To test if these alternative synthetic datasets offer useful foundational skills, we further fine-tuned the models on the AWT data collected from the AppWorld environment. Even with this real-environment supervision, their final performance was significantly lower than that of models trained on ESAT data.

5 Conclusion

We presented ESAT, an environment-free pipeline that synthesizes training data for API-calling agents using only API specifications. By combining coverage-aware task generation, a state-consistent LLM-based API simulator, and a trajectory-level LLM judge, ESAT produces high-quality, multi-step trajectories without using any functional environment. Evaluations on the challenging AppWorld and OfficeBench benchmarks demonstrate substantial performance gains across models ranging from 1.7B to 27B parameters. On AppWorld, models trained on synthetic ESAT data outperform the models trained on trajectories collected from the real environment. On both benchmarks, we are able to either outperform or approach the performance of GPT-4o using significantly smaller models with 4B to 8B parameters. These results establish our environment-free data synthesis pipeline as a highly effective and scalable solution for training API-calling agents.

Appendices

Appendix A Data Statistics of ESAT-AW7

A.1 Synthesis Throughput and Yield

Task synthesis throughput.

Table 7 reports the number of tasks surviving each stage of the synthesis pipeline. Starting from 29,676 candidate tasks produced by the task generator, the initial judge accepts 14,361 (48.39%), filtering out roughly 52% of the generations as ill-formed, unsolvable, or inconsistent with the requested bucket attributes. The rewriting step then successfully reformulates 13,805 of these into concise, intent-level requests, with a small fraction (556 tasks, 1.87% of the original pool) discarded due to rewriting failures. Finally, the second judge re-validates the rewritten tasks against the original specifications, approving 12,242 tasks (41.25% of the initial pool). For any rewritten tasks rejected by this second judge, the pipeline falls back to the corresponding initial tasks for trajectory synthesis.

Trajectory generation throughput.

Table 7 reports the yield of the trajectory synthesis stage. Out of 14,361 input tasks, the teacher agent successfully completes 11,445 trajectories (79.70%), meaning the agent terminates with a final answer regardless of its correctness. The judge then filters these completed trajectories for solution quality, retaining 9,352 trajectories (65.13% of the input tasks) for supervised fine-tuning. Across all 245,762 simulated API calls issued during generation, only 15,037 (6.12%) required a retry from the simulator due to schema or semantic validation failures. This low retry rate indicates that the simulator produces well-formed and consistent responses on the first attempt in the majority of cases.

A.2 Failure Analysis

Failure type of trajectory generation.

Table 8 breaks down the 5,009 discarded trajectories by failure mode. The dominant cause is simulation failure (45.38%). Most of these failures stem from simulator timeouts when an agent issues too many simulated API calls within a single step. The remainder occur when the simulator cannot produce a response that passes both the schema check and the LLM-as-a-judge consistency check within the retry budget. The second largest category is judge rejection (41.78%). These trajectories complete end-to-end but are filtered out by the LLM judge for incorrect or low-quality solutions; this represents the intended quality-control mechanism of the pipeline rather than a pipeline error. Agent’s unexpected App use (10.72%) occurs when the agent calls an API outside the expected set derived from the task, prompting early termination. The remaining failures are minor: agent model execution failures (2.00%) are caused by transient errors from the teacher LLM serving stack, such as rate limits or decoding errors, and max solve steps exceeded (0.06%) happens when the agent fails to terminate within the step budget, while three unexpected runtime errors (0.06%) account for the remainder. Overall, judge filtering and simulator-side validation account for roughly 87% of all discarded trajectories, with agent-side failures contributing only a small tail.

A.3 Dataset Diversity and Coverage

Task distribution.

Figures 3(a), 3(b), 3(c) and 3(d) present the distribution of the generated tasks used for trajectory synthesis across four dimensions. While the generated tasks exhibit fairly uniform coverage across task difficulty levels, action types, and task focus categories, the distribution is skewed regarding the number of apps involved, with two- and three-app tasks being significantly less frequent than single-app tasks. This could be due to the inherent difficulty an LLM-based task generator faces when composing meaningful multi-app tasks. Additionally, it is likely that this distribution reflects a naturally non-uniform distribution of tasks in the real world.

Trajectory distribution.

To ensure our synthetic dataset captures a diverse and balanced range of agentic capabilities, we analyze the distribution of the successfully generated trajectories across four dimensions, as illustrated in Figures 3(e), 3(f), 3(g) and 3(h). The generated dataset exhibits broad coverage across task difficulty levels, action types, and task focus categories. However, the distribution is skewed regarding the number of apps involved, with two- and three-app tasks being significantly less frequent than single-app tasks.

API coverage.

To measure the diversity and breadth of our synthesized dataset, we evaluate API coverage by counting the number of unique APIs successfully invoked within the generated trajectories. We compute the coverage ratio across varying frequency thresholds, calculating how many APIs appear at least NN times (where N∈{1,2,3,5,10,20,50}N\in\{1,2,3,5,10,20,50\}). As shown in Figure 4, our pipeline achieves near-complete coverage. Of the 340 APIs from the AppWorld environment, 339 (99.7%) appear in at least one successful trajectory, with only a single API never invoked, and 323 (95%) are utilized at least five times. These high coverage rates demonstrate that our inverse-frequency sampling strategy effectively prevents the data distribution from collapsing onto a narrow subset of APIs, ensuring the agent learns robust and generalized API-usage capabilities.

Appendix B Data Statistics of ESAT-S52

B.1 Synthesis Throughput and Yield

Task synthesis throughput.

Table 10 outlines task retention at each phase of the ESAT-S52 synthesis pipeline. From an initial batch of 32,009 generated tasks, the first judge preserves 10,509 (32.83%), effectively discarding approximately 67% for being unsolvable, improperly formatted, or mismatched with their designated bucket attributes. These surviving tasks undergo a rewriting phase to create concise, intent-focused requests. This phase yields 9,171 successful reformulations, dropping 1,338 tasks (4.18% of the total pool) due to rewriting errors. Finally, a secondary judge cross-checks these rewritten prompts against the original criteria, resulting in a curated pool of 7,072 tasks (22.09% of the initial count). When a rewritten task is rejected, its corresponding initial task is retained for trajectory synthesis.

Trajectory generation throughput.

Table 10 details the yield of the trajectory synthesis phase for ESAT-S52. From an initial set of 10,509 input tasks, the teacher agent successfully completes 8,020 trajectories (76.32%), meaning the agent reached a final answer irrespective of its actual correctness. A subsequent quality filter by the judge narrows these down, retaining 6,265 high-quality trajectories (59.62% of the original input) to be used for supervised fine-tuning. Furthermore, out of the 154,317 simulated API calls executed during this process, only 6,062 (3.93%) necessitated a retry due to schema or semantic validation errors. This low retry rate demonstrates that the simulator reliably generates well-formed and consistent responses on the first attempt.

B.2 Failure Analysis

Failure type of trajectory generation.

Table 11 breaks down the 4,244 discarded trajectories by failure mode. The dominant cause is judge rejection (41.35%). These trajectories complete end-to-end but are filtered out by the LLM judge for incorrect or low-quality solutions; this represents the intended quality-control mechanism of the pipeline rather than a pipeline error. The second largest category is simulation failure (28.30%). Most of these failures stem from simulator timeouts when an agent issues too many simulated API calls within a single step, along with cases where the simulator cannot produce a response that passes both the schema check and the LLM-as-a-judge consistency check within the retry budget. Agent’s unexpected App use (22.05%) occurs when the agent calls an API outside the expected set derived from the task, prompting early termination. Agent model execution failures (8.25%) are caused by transient errors from the teacher LLM serving stack, such as rate limits or decoding errors. The remaining failures are negligible: max solve steps exceeded (0.02%) happens when the agent fails to terminate within the step budget, and a single unexpected runtime error (0.02%) accounts for the rest.

B.3 Dataset Diversity and Coverage

Task distribution.

Figures 5(a), 5(b), 5(c) and 5(d) present the distribution of the generated tasks used for trajectory synthesis across four dimensions. While the generated tasks exhibit fairly uniform coverage across task focus categories, action types, and difficulty levels, the distribution is distinctly skewed regarding the number of apps involved. Single-app tasks make up the majority at 64%, with two-app and three-app tasks comprising 26% and 11% of the dataset, respectively. This could be due to the inherent difficulty an LLM-based task generator faces when composing meaningful multi-app tasks. Additionally, it is likely that this distribution reflects a naturally non-uniform distribution of tasks in the real world.

Trajectory distribution.

To ensure our synthetic dataset captures a diverse and balanced range of agentic capabilities, we analyze the distribution of the successfully generated trajectories across four dimensions, as illustrated in Figures 5(e), 5(f), 5(g) and 5(h). The dataset exhibits broad coverage across task difficulty levels (easy 31%, medium 31%, hard 38%), action types (mixed 38%, read 32%, write 29%), and task focus categories (constraint satisfaction 25%, derivation 21%, iteration 28%, open 27%). As in the task pool, however, the distribution is skewed regarding the number of apps involved, with two-app (14%) and three-app (3%) trajectories being substantially less frequent than single-app trajectories (83%).

API coverage.

To assess the diversity and breadth of our synthesized dataset, we measure API coverage by tracking the number of unique APIs successfully invoked throughout the generated trajectories. We determine this coverage using various frequency thresholds, calculating the proportion of APIs that appear at least NN times (where N∈{1,2,3,5,10,20,50}N\in\{1,2,3,5,10,20,50\}). As illustrated in Figure 6, our pipeline achieves near-complete coverage across the environment. Out of the 1,017 APIs distributed across our 52 synthetic apps, 1,013 (99.6%) are called in at least one successful trajectory, and 951 (93.5%) are utilized at least five times. These high coverage rates confirm that our inverse-frequency sampling strategy effectively prevents the data distribution from collapsing onto a narrow subset of popular endpoints, ensuring the agent develops robust and generalized API-calling capabilities.

Appendix C Data Statistics of OfficeBench

C.1 Synthesis Throughput and Yield

Task synthesis throughput.

Table 13 reports the number of tasks surviving each stage of the synthesis pipeline for OfficeBench. Starting from 11,797 candidate tasks produced by the task generator, the initial judge accepts 3,465 (29.37%), filtering out roughly 70% of generations as ill-formed, unsolvable, or inconsistent with the requested bucket attributes. The rewriting step then successfully reformulates 3,336 of these into concise, intent-level requests, with only a minor drop-off due to rewriting failures. Finally, the final judge re-validates the rewritten tasks against the original specifications, retaining 2,380 tasks (20.17% of the initial pool). In cases where a rewritten task is rejected during this final validation, the pipeline falls back to using the corresponding initial task for trajectory synthesis.

Trajectory generation throughput.

Table 13 reports the yield of the trajectory synthesis stage for OfficeBench. Out of 3,465 input tasks, the teacher agent successfully completes 1,889 trajectories (54.52%), where completion indicates that the agent terminates with a final answer regardless of correctness. The judge then filters these completed trajectories for overall solution quality, retaining 1,711 trajectories (49.38% of the input tasks) for the final dataset. Across all 12,084 simulated API calls issued during this generation phase, only 919 (7.61%) required a retry from the simulator due to schema or semantic validation failures. This low retry rate indicates that the simulator is highly reliable, producing well-formed and consistent responses on the first attempt in the vast majority of cases.

C.2 Failure Analysis

Failure type of trajectory generation.

Table 14 breaks down the 1,754 discarded trajectories by failure mode for OfficeBench. The dominant failure mode is agent model execution failure, accounting for 77.42% of all failures. These occur when the teacher agent itself fails to produce a valid action or terminate properly during trajectory generation. The second largest category is judge rejection (10.15%): these trajectories complete end-to-end but are filtered out by the LLM judge for incorrect or low-quality solutions, reflecting the strict, intended quality-control signal of our pipeline. Next, simulation failure makes up 8.61% of discarded trajectories, typically occurring when the simulator cannot produce a response that passes the schema and consistency checks within the retry budget, or due to simulator timeouts. Finally, max solve steps exceeded accounts for 3.82%, which occurs when the agent fails to terminate within the allocated step budget (30), indicating that for a small subset of tasks the agent either gets stuck in an execution loop or the task requires a longer sequence of actions than anticipated. Overall, the failure distribution shows that most discarded trajectories stem from agent-side execution issues, followed by quality filtering, with infrastructure and step-budget failures making up a smaller share.

C.3 Dataset Diversity and Coverage

Task distribution.

Figures 7(a), 7(b), 7(c) and 7(d) present the distribution of the generated tasks used for trajectory synthesis across four dimensions. While the generated tasks exhibit fairly uniform coverage across task focus categories (ranging narrowly from 24% to 26%), action types (spanning 31% to 35%), and difficulty levels (distributed evenly between 32% and 34%), the distribution displays a distinct pattern regarding the number of apps involved. In contrast to single-app dominated datasets, two-app tasks represent the plurality at 40%, with single-app and three-app tasks comprising 35% and 25% of the dataset, respectively. This reflects a structural emphasis within ESAT-OB on multi-app orchestration, purposefully challenging the agent with complex, cross-application workflows that mirror advanced, real-world user intents.

Trajectory distribution.

To ensure our synthetic dataset captures a diverse range of agentic capabilities within the OfficeBench domain, we analyze the distribution of the successfully generated trajectories across our five configuration axes, as illustrated in Figure 7. The generated dataset exhibits a highly balanced distribution across its qualitative dimensions. Task difficulty (Figure 7(g)) is exceptionally uniform, with “easy,” “medium,” and “hard” tasks comprising 34%, 32%, and 34% of the dataset, respectively. Action types (Figure 7(f)) are similarly well-represented, where “mixed” read/write actions form the largest share at 43%, while pure “read” (30%) and “write” (27%) actions are nearly evenly split. Task focus categories (Figure 7(e)) show a slight tilt toward “iteration” (29%) and “open” (28%) tasks, while still maintaining solid representation for “derivation” (24%) and “constraint satisfaction” (19%).

API coverage.

To measure the breadth of our synthesized dataset within the OfficeBench domain, we evaluate the API coverage by counting the number of unique APIs successfully invoked. As shown in Figure 8, out of the 20 total APIs available in the environment, 70% (14 APIs) appear in at least one successful trajectory. The coverage remains highly stable across higher frequency thresholds, with 70% (14 APIs) utilized at least 5 times and only a slight decline to 65% (13 APIs) at 10 times. Furthermore, 60% (12 APIs) appear 50 times or more, ensuring deep and repeated exposure to core functionalities. We note that six specific APIs are entirely absent from the successfully generated trajectories: four in Excel (convert_to_pdf, create_new_file, delete_cell, and set_cell) and two in PDF (convert_to_image and convert_to_word). Nevertheless, the strong and stable retention of the remaining APIs demonstrates that our sampling strategy effectively captures the vast majority of the OfficeBench action space.

Appendix D Implementation Details

Data synthesis.

For task synthesis (Stage 1), we use GLM-4.7-FP8 as both the task generator and the LLM judge that validates generated tasks. For trajectory synthesis (Stage 2), GLM-5.1-FP8 serves as the teacher agent and the API simulator, and the maximum number of agent steps per trajectory is set to 50 for AppWorld and 30 for OfficeBench. Trajectories that exceed this limit are aborted as described in the trajectory termination rules. For trajectory filtering (Stage 3), we use Gemini-3.1-Pro as the LLM judge.

Training.

We fine-tune all models with supervised learning on full multi-turn trajectories. Each trajectory is decomposed into individual turns, and the model is trained to predict the tokens of the current turn conditioned on all preceding turns, with the loss masked out over the context tokens. We use the AdamW (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019) optimizer with a learning rate of 2⋅10−52\cdot 10^{-5}, a linear decay schedule, and a warmup ratio of 1%. Training is performed with a context length of 32,768 tokens and a per-device batch size of 1. For models smaller than 14B parameters, training is distributed across 8 H100 GPUs, whereas for models 14B and larger, we utilize 8 B200 GPUs. We leverage the Transformers library (Wolf et al., 2020) for model implementation and use PyTorch native FSDP2 for distributed training. To improve training efficiency, we apply sequence packing, which concatenates roughly 4 samples into a single sequence on average. We train for 10 epochs by default, except for the Qwen3.5 family, where we observed overfitting beyond 5 epochs and therefore reduce training to 5 epochs. For the first stage of training on synthetic data, we use both the AppWorld train and dev splits for checkpoint selection. For the second stage, which further fine-tunes the model on the AppWorld train split, we keep all hyperparameters identical and select the best checkpoint based on the dev split alone. For OfficeBench, as there is no dedicated development set, we apply the exact same hyperparameters used for AppWorld.

Inference and evaluation.

For efficient, high-throughput inference, we evaluate all models using vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023). During evaluation, we set the sampling temperature to 1.0. Following the evaluation protocol of AppWorld and OfficeBench, the maximum number of agent steps is capped at 50 for AppWorld and 30 for OfficeBench. For both benchmarks, we generate 8 independent samples per task and report the average pass@1 metric to robustly measure agent performance.

Appendix E Training with AppWorld Train splits

We investigate the effect of upsampling filtered teacher trajectories on student model performance. Specifically, we use the 90 training tasks from the AppWorld train split and prompt a teacher agent to generate 8 solution trajectories per task. We then filter out trajectories corresponding to incorrect solutions, which results in a variable number of valid trajectories per task (at most 8). To examine whether balancing the per-task contribution matters, we compare two settings: (i) w/o upsampling, which directly uses the filtered trajectories as-is, and (ii) w/ upsampling, which randomly duplicates the remaining trajectories until each task contributes exactly 8 trajectories. We fine-tune four Qwen variants (Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, Qwen3.5-4B, and Qwen3.5-9B) under both settings and evaluate on the Test-N and Test-C splits.

Table 15 reports the results. Overall, upsampling does not yield consistent improvements over the non-upsampled baseline. On Qwen3.5-9B, upsampling slightly improves Test-N accuracy (73.14 vs. 71.21) but marginally degrades Test-C (51.89 vs. 53.84). For the remaining three models, upsampling underperforms the baseline on both splits, with the largest gap observed on Qwen3.5-4B Test-C (42.39 vs. 46.70). These results suggest that naively duplicating trajectories to balance per-task counts does not help and can in fact hurt generalization, likely because duplicated trajectories reduce sample diversity and amplify the influence of tasks with few valid trajectories. We therefore adopt the non-upsampled setting in our subsequent experiments.

Appendix F Full Experimental Results

We present the complete evaluation results for our experiments in this section. Table 16 details the comprehensive performance on the AppWorld benchmark, reporting both Task Goal Completion (TGC) and Scenario Goal Completion (SGC) metrics across the Test-Normal and Test-Challenge splits. Similarly, Table 17 provides the full pass rate breakdown for 2-app, 3-app, and overall tasks on the OfficeBench dataset. For both benchmarks, we report the mean performance along with standard deviations across 8 independent inference runs for all evaluated models and training data configurations.

Appendix G Task Synthesis

The goal of task synthesis is to produce a large and diverse pool of natural, multi-step user tasks that can be solved using only the available APIs. The only input to this stage is a set of API specifications, where each specification provides an API’s name, purpose, input-parameter schema, and output-response schema. From these specifications, we generate, judge, and rewrite candidate tasks. We use a single LLM, GLM-4.7-FP8 (Zeng et al., 2025), for all three roles (generator, judge, and rewriter) by varying the prompt.

G.1 Bucketized generation.

To ensure broad and balanced coverage of the task space, generation is organized into a combinatorial grid of configuration buckets. Each bucket is a tuple (difficulty, action_type, task_focus, num_apps, [min_apis, max_apis]), where (i) difficulty ∈{easy,medium,hard}\in\{\textsc{easy},\textsc{medium},\textsc{hard}\} controls the depth of reasoning required (Table 19); (ii) action_type ∈{read,write,mixed}\in\{\textsc{read},\textsc{write},\textsc{mixed}\} controls the mix of GET vs. POST/PATCH/DELETE calls (Table 20); (iii) task_focus (e.g., constraint satisfaction, derivation, iteration, open) controls the high-level reasoning pattern (Table 21); (iv) num_apps ∈{1,2,3}\in\{1,2,3\} specifies the number of distinct apps a task must span; and (v) [min_apis,max_apis][\text{min\_apis},\text{max\_apis}] specifies the per-app API budget. The per-app API budgets are pinned to match the typical per-app load needed at each app count: for num_apps=1\text{num\_apps}=1, we sweep five pinned values [k,k][k,k] for k∈{2,…,6}k\in\{2,\dots,6\}; for num_apps=2\text{num\_apps}=2, we use ranges {[1,2],[2,3],[3,4]}\{[1,2],[2,3],[3,4]\}; and for num_apps=3\text{num\_apps}=3, we use {[1,2],[2,3]}\{[1,2],[2,3]\}. This yields 3⋅3⋅4⋅(5+3+2)=3603\cdot 3\cdot 4\cdot(5+3+2)=360 buckets in total. Buckets are processed sequentially in a random order, and each bucket targets a fixed number of accepted tasks, NbucketN_{\text{bucket}}.

For each bucket, the pipeline issues ⌈Nbucket/nper_call⌉\lceil N_{\text{bucket}}/n_{\text{per\_call}}\rceil parallel calls to the task generator LLM, each asked to produce nper_calln_{\text{per\_call}} distinct candidate tasks. For hard buckets (difficulty=hard\text{difficulty}=\textsc{hard}, num_apps=3\text{num\_apps}=3, or num_apps⋅min_apis>5\text{num\_apps}\cdot\text{min\_apis}>5), we double the maximum-completion-tokens budget for the generator, judge, and rewriter to accommodate longer outputs.

G.2 Inverse frequency-based sampling.

To prevent the generator from collapsing onto a small set of apps and APIs, we maintain running usage counts c⁡(a)c(a) and c⁡(α)c(\alpha) for every app aa and every API α\alpha across all tasks generated so far. Coverage is refreshed at the start of each bucket from this job’s own outputs. When constructing a generator call:

  1. 1.

    App sampling. We sample num_apps apps without replacement using p⁡(a)∝1/(1+c⁡(a)),p(a)\propto 1/(1+c(a)), which assigns the highest probability to the least-used apps.

  2. 2.

    API spotlighting. For each selected app, we provide the generator with the full set of API specifications for that app, but additionally surface a list of the top-10 APIs ranked by inverse coverage as focus APIs. These are listed under a dedicated section of the prompt with instructions to prioritize them, while still leaving the generator free to use any of the provided APIs to satisfy other requirements.

  3. 3.

    Prompt assembly. The selected app/API specification, the focus-API list, the bucket-specific difficulty, action-type, task-focus clauses (Tables 19, 20 and 21), and the per-app API-count range are inserted into the task generation prompt template shown in .

G.3 Task judging.

Each surviving candidate is then evaluated by an LLM judge that is given the same API specification and the exact requirements section that was shown to the generator (the universal requirements plus the bucket-specific difficulty, action-type, task-focus, coverage, and required-apps clauses. Refer to ). The judge is instructed to think through how the task would be solved, since this is necessary for it to assess API coverage, difficulty, and focus compliance, and then output a single yes or no verdict. Tasks receiving a No are excluded from downstream stages.

G.4 Task rewriting.

Tasks generated directly from API specifications often suffer from procedural verbosity: the generator tends to enumerate intermediate steps that any agent would infer on its own (e.g., “first look up X, then check Y, then if Z…”). To convert these into natural, intent-level user requests, every task that passes the judge is rewritten by a second LLM call. The rewriter is shown (i) the original task, (ii) the same task-requirements block used by the generator and judge, and (iii) only the API specification of the APIs covered by the task (rather than the full bucket-level pool) so that it stays focused on preserving the original API coverage. To anchor the desired writing style, we append three in-context examples to the prompt body that pair a verbose, procedural original with its compact, goal-oriented rewrite (, ). The rewriter is explicitly instructed to preserve every detail the user actually cares about, while stripping setup phrases and obvious intermediate steps. Table 18 shows two representative before-and-after pairs. In both cases, the initial generated task reads as a detailed, multi-sentence walkthrough that explicitly enumerates the steps the agent should take. The rewritten task preserves the same underlying intent, but expresses it as a short, natural user request that omits the procedural scaffolding.

G.5 Final re-judging.

Because rewriting can occasionally drop a required entity or change the task’s scope, every rewritten task is passed through the judge a second time with the same prompt template. Only tasks that pass both judging rounds are added to the final pool. Tasks rejected at the final judge stage are recorded with their original generation metadata for diagnostic purposes but excluded from the task pool.

G.6 Prompts for Task Synthesis

Given the documentation of a sampled subset of APIs, a target difficulty / action-type / task-focus configuration, and a list of negative examples (already-generated tasks) and under-utilized APIs, the model produces {num_tasks} candidate tasks per call. The configurable clauses ({difficulty_clause}, {action_type_clause}, {task_focus_clause}) are sampled from the variants enumerated in Tables 19, 20 and 21.

Appendix H Simulator Details

This section provides a detailed description of the LLM-based API simulator used during trajectory synthesis. The simulator is purely text-based: there is no real backend, no database, and no network call. Its job is to take an API call issued by the teacher agent and produce a JSON response that (i) conforms to the documented response schema, (ii) is internally consistent with all responses returned so far in the same task, and (iii) plausibly reflects the user profile and the current task.

H.1 Per-Task, Per-App Histories

For each task, the simulator maintains an independent rolling history of accepted (call, response) pairs for each app. Restricting the history to a single app sharply reduces prompt length and prevents irrelevant entities from leaking into one app’s simulated state.

When constructing a prompt, the simulator formats the most recent calls in this app’s history as “Call 11 …Call NN,” each entry containing the API signature, the input parameters, and the previously simulated response. The history is capped at a configurable maximum number of calls, but in practice the per-task length stays well below this cap. When a task finishes, its histories are explicitly cleared, so simulator state never leaks between tasks.

H.2 Deterministic Input Validation

Inputs of an API call are validated against the API specification using rules that mirror the validation a real backend would apply. If any check fails, the simulator returns an error message without calling the LLM. The checks are:

  • •

    Unknown parameters not present in the endpoint’s parameter list.

  • •

    Missing required parameters for which no default was filled in.

  • •

    Type mismatches, with the same scalar coercions a real backend would perform (e.g., the string “42” is accepted for an integer field, but a boolean is not; container types require an exact match).

  • •

    Constraint violations, including length bounds, numeric bounds (with strict and non-strict inequalities), enumerated value sets, and email-format checks.

Surfacing these errors deterministically rather than asking the LLM to invent them ensures that the agent always sees the same error message for the same malformed call, which makes downstream filtering and learning more stable.

H.3 Prompt Construction

For every call that reaches the LLM, the simulator builds a two-message conversation: a fixed system prompt that lays out the simulator’s role, the six categories of context it receives, and the rules it must follow (, with the rules block in and ); and a per-call user prompt assembled from the template in . The user prompt contains, in this order: the fully qualified API name, a JSON dump of the inputs (with defaults filled and the page-limit cap applied), the full API specification (description, parameters, response schema), the dedicated response-schema block extracted from the specification, which gives the model a clean target for its output, the task description that the teacher agent is currently solving, the per-app interaction history described in Section H.1; the user profile (first name, last name, email, phone number) drawn from the fictitious supervisor record assigned to this task, and the frozen current date and time. The model is then asked to return raw JSON.

H.4 Output Schema Validation

Once the LLM’s simulated response is received, we first strip any markdown code fences that the model may have emitted in violation of the rules, and then attempt a strict JSON parse. On parse failure, a structured feedback message containing the raw response and the parser error is appended to the conversation (Section H.6). After parsing, the JSON value is structurally compared against both (i) the documented success schema and (ii) the canonical error schema {"message":string}\{\texttt{"message"}:\text{string}\}. The response is accepted if it conforms to either, since both are legitimate outcomes according to the simulator rules (). If neither schema matches, both errors are bundled into a structured feedback message, and the loop in Section H.6 retries.

H.5 Simulator-judge

A structurally valid response is still subject to a semantic check, but only for read-only (HTTP GET) APIs. Write APIs (POST, PATCH, DELETE) are accepted as soon as they pass structural validation. This is because their semantic content is typically a simple acknowledgment whose validity is fully captured by the schema, and because gating writes behind a semantic judge would double the LLM cost for state-mutating calls without a proportionate gain in quality. For read APIs, the simulator invokes a separate LLM judge using the system prompt in and the user prompt in . The judge receives the exact same context as the simulator (specification, inputs, task, history, user profile, and current date/time) alongside the candidate response, and is tasked with returning a JSON verdict containing three fields: a boolean validity flag, a list of issues, and a free-text suggestion block. The judge employs a bounded retry loop to handle any JSON-parsing failures of its own, after which it raises a simulation-failed error.

H.6 Retry Loop With Structured Feedback

The structural check and the judge feed into a single retry loop with two independent attempt budgets: a format budget for JSON-parse and schema-validation failures, and a semantic budget for judge rejections. After any rejection, the conversation is extended with two messages: an assistant message containing the rejected response verbatim, and a user message containing the structured feedback. For format failures the feedback names the precise error (parse exception, missing keys, type mismatch) and re-states the two acceptable shapes (success schema or error object). For semantic failures the feedback enumerates the judge’s listed issues and reproduces its suggestions verbatim. This in-context conversational format gives the model both a concrete negative example and an actionable hint. We find that it converges within the budget for the vast majority of calls. Once either budget is exhausted, we terminate trajectory synthesis.

H.7 Prompt for Simulator

Appendix K Synthetic Application Suite

To broaden the application coverage of AppWorld beyond its original nine productivity-focused apps, we construct a suite of 52 synthetic apps spanning ten functional categories. Each application is modeled as a REST API consistent with AppWorld’s structural conventions and is fully specified with typed endpoints, parameter constraints, and structured response schemas. The suite comprises 1,017 API endpoints across the 52 apps.

K.1 Domain Selection

The 52 app domains were selected through a manual curation process guided by two principles: real-world fidelity, where each domain corresponds to a widely used category of software, and functional diversity, where the collection as a whole requires agents to exercise qualitatively different interaction patterns, data models, and reasoning skills. Domains were selected to complement and extend AppWorld’s existing application coverage while minimizing redundancy with previously supported domains.

We manually defined a seed set of 10 broad functional categories and identified specific app types within each category. For each app type we specified a short description and a list of key agent-facing functionalities. shows a representative entry from our seed set. Using these manually defined entries as in-context examples, we then prompted Gemini-2.5-Pro to expand the list with additional domains following the same format and coverage criteria, specifically requesting diversity across the remaining domain space and avoiding overlap with the seed entries.

Table 22 summarizes the ten functional domains and their constituent app counts for the 52 synthetic apps.

K.2 API Schema Design

For each domain, we generated a complete REST API schema by prompting Gemini-2.5-Pro with (1) the target domain description drawn from our domain taxonomy, and (2) six representative ⟨𝚋𝚊𝚗𝚔𝚒𝚗𝚐​_​𝚊𝚙𝚙⟩\langle\mathtt{banking\_app}\rangle APIs from AppWorld as structural few-shot examples. The six examples were deliberately selected to cover the full range of structural patterns that appear in the suite: a public authentication API (login), a simple authenticated GET (show_account), a resource creation POST with required and optional parameters (create_transaction), a complex list API with filters, pagination, and sort_by (show_transactions), a stateful action on a sub-resource (like_transaction), and a sub-resource GET by ID (show_payment_card). shows two of these six examples.

Prompt structure.

The full Gemini prompt is structured in five parts, shown in abbreviated form in . The domain name and description from the domain taxonomy () are injected at the top of the prompt as a target header (Part 1), which tells Gemini which specific domain to generate and which key workflows to cover. Part (2) specifies the required app_description and the API coverage requirements (core CRUD, sub-resources, actions, search/filter, social features, notifications, payments, file downloads). Part (3) defines the exact JSON output schema for each API object and each parameter object. Part (4) states mandatory conventions: the access_token parameter ordering rule, the 10 standard auth/account APIs every app must include, pagination conventions, and response schema placeholder formats. Part (5) provides the six ⟨𝚋𝚊𝚗𝚔𝚒𝚗𝚐​_​𝚊𝚙𝚙⟩\langle\mathtt{banking\_app}\rangle example APIs. A diversity constraint is appended when generating multiple apps in sequence, listing already-generated app names that must not be duplicated.

Verification.

After each Gemini response, a rule-based verifier checks 13 structural invariants before accepting the schema: all required top-level keys are present; all 10 standard APIs are included; each API has the seven required fields; paths start with /<app_name>/; HTTP methods are valid; access_token is absent on public APIs and present on all others; access_token does not appear after optional parameters; response_schemas has both success and failure keys; all parameter types are from the allowed set; and at least one domain-specific API exists beyond the standard 10. Schemas that fail verification are discarded and regenerated up to a configurable retry limit.

Schema structure.

Each API is defined by eight fields: app_name, api_name, path, method (GET / POST/ PATCH / DELETE), description, parameters, response_schemas, and canary_string. Specifications are authored using four Python helpers that enforce structural uniformity across all applications: api_() constructs a full API entry; p() constructs a typed parameter; tok() is shorthand for the standard access_token parameter; and paged() appends the three standard pagination parameters to a parameter list.

Design conventions.

We enforced the following conventions across all 52 applications to ensure a consistent interface vocabulary:

  • •

    Authentication. Every application exposes a login API returning an access_token, which is required on all authenticated APIs, mirroring the pattern in the original AppWorld applications.

  • •

    Pagination. All list-returning APIs accept page_index (0-based, default 0), page_limit (default 5), and sort_by (attribute prefixed with +/- for ascending/descending order).

  • •

    Type-safe response schemas. Response schemas use typed placeholders: ‘‘string’’ for text fields, 1 for integer IDs, 0.0 for floats, ‘‘2019-01-01T00:00:00’’ for timestamps, and ‘‘user@example.com’’ for email fields, never domain-specific invented values.

  • •

    Constraint notation. Parameter constraints follow a strict vocabulary: ‘‘length >= 1’’, ‘‘value >= 0.0, <= 5.0’’, ‘‘value in [’a’, ’b’]’’, and ‘‘value is email address’’. No other formats are valid.

  • •

    Nested sub-resources. Where a resource logically contains an embedded sub-resource (e.g., a ride has a driver; a booking has a host), the response schema includes a nested object rather than flattening all fields.

  • •

    Failure responses. The failure branch of every API is uniformly {‘‘message’’: ‘‘string’’} across all 52 applications.

K.3 Schema Conversion

The Python specification files are serialized to a consolidated JSON file and then converted per app into AppWorld’s canonical format using Gemini-3.1-Pro. For each app, a structured prompt is constructed containing: (1) reference examples from the original AppWorld ⟨𝚖𝚞𝚜𝚒𝚌​_​𝚊𝚙𝚙⟩\langle\mathtt{music\_app}\rangle schema as few-shot demonstrations; (2) explicit formatting rules for description style, constraint vocabulary, and response schema placeholder conventions; and (3) the full API specification for the target application. Gemini returns a JSON object mapping each api_name to its complete AppWorld-format entry.

Following conversion, each API entry is annotated with a canary string of the form appworld:{md5_prefix}:{uuid}, where the MD5 prefix is the first seven hex characters of the application name’s hash and the UUID is freshly generated per API. Canary strings serve two purposes: they enable traceability of downstream generated data back to its source application, and they provide a signal for detecting schema memorization during model evaluation. The conversion pipeline includes automatic retry on JSON parse failures and falls back to a deterministic structural converter for any applications where LLM conversion fails, ensuring all 52 applications produce valid output.

K.4 AppWorld Integration

The converted schemas are consumed by a deterministic code generation script that produces a deployable AppWorld module for each app, comprising five files: __init__.py (module initialization), info.toml (metadata with app_type = ‘‘synthetic’’ marker), models.py (SQLModel database models with a standard User table), apis.py (FastAPI API stubs wired to AppWorld’s shared authentication library), and responses.py (Pydantic response model definitions). The 52 synthetic applications are registered as SYNTHETIC_APP_NAMES separately from the 9 original ORIGINAL_APP_NAMES, and the app_type = ‘‘synthetic’’ marker enables controlled ablation studies over application subsets during evaluation.

Appendix L Example Agent Trajectories

To illustrate the behavior of our agent in the simulated environment, we present three representative end-to-end trajectories in Figures 9, 10 and 11. The examples span varying levels of complexity, ranging from a single-app task (⟨𝚋𝚊𝚗𝚔𝚒𝚗𝚐​_​𝚊𝚙𝚙⟩\langle\mathtt{banking\_app}\rangle, 15 steps) to a cross-app workflow involving three apps (⟨𝚎𝚡𝚙𝚎𝚗𝚜𝚎𝚜​_​𝚊𝚙𝚙⟩\langle\mathtt{expenses\_app}\rangle, ⟨𝚗𝚘𝚝𝚎​_​𝚊𝚙𝚙⟩\langle\mathtt{note\_app}\rangle, and ⟨𝚊𝚌𝚝𝚒𝚘𝚗​_​𝚒𝚝𝚎𝚖​_​𝚕𝚒𝚜𝚝​_​𝚊𝚙𝚙⟩\langle\mathtt{action\_item\_list\_app}\rangle, 25 steps). In each trajectory, the agent discovers relevant APIs through the documentation interface, retrieves credentials from the supervisor app, authenticates, and chains multi-step API calls to fulfill the user’s request. All API responses are produced by the LLM-based simulator. For privacy, we mask sensitive virtual user information, including names, email addresses, passwords, access tokens, card numbers, and CVVs, replacing them with **** or generic placeholders such as user@example.com. Other fields such as API schemas, product and brand names, monetary amounts, and resource identifiers are kept verbatim to preserve the reasoning context. These examples are synthetic benchmark tasks and do not correspond to real users, real accounts, real credentials, real payment instruments, or real financial transactions.
